translations.note: A false etymology traditional in Latin grammarians: cura (care) is derived as if from cor (heart) + uro (I burn), since care burns the heart. Burton calls it 'the common Etymology'. The English cannot keep the pun, so the translation spells out the derivation.
translations.text: Cura, care, as if from 'cor uro', I burn the heart

translations.note: A folk etymology: cura (care) is derived from cor uro, 'I burn the heart'. The English cannot reproduce the play, so the Latin is kept and the sense given.
translations.text: Cura, as if cor uro, I burn the heart

source.author: Palladas
source.basis: The wording matches the well-known epigram in the Greek Anthology that begins 'Δακρυχέων γενόμην καὶ δακρύσας ἀποθνῄσκω', which is usually attributed to Palladas.

1.2.3.10-f10.text: Δακρυχέων γενόμην, καὶ δακρύσας ἀποθνῄσκω, ὦ γένος ἀνθρώπων πολυδάκρυτον, ἀσθενές, οἰκτρόν

translations.note: This is an epigram from the Greek Anthology. Burton runs the first and third lines together and leaves out the line in between ('and I found my whole life amid many tears'). He adds his own Latin version, 'Lachrymans natus sum, & lachrymans morior, &c.' The English at the point where the note is anchored renders Pliny, not this epigram.

source.author: Palladas
source.basis: The wording matches the well-known epigram in the Greek Anthology that begins 'Δακρυχέων γενόμην καὶ δακρύσας ἀποθνῄσκω', which is usually attributed to Palladas.

translations.text: Weeping I was born, and having wept I die; O race of men, much-lamented, weak, pitiable

translations.note: Greek epigram. Burton's own Latin rendering follows in the paragraph (Lachrymans natus sum, & lachrymans morior); it is not English. His English at the anchor gives only the gist of Pliny's description of birth, not this passage.
translations.text: Weeping I was born, and weeping I die, O race of men, much-wept, weak, pitiable
